issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, this appraisal is a poor thematic fit because it implies an interpersonal perpetrator threat ('who will harm you') rather than danger from impersonal environmental forces. The rest of the profile is built around disaster-related ongoing danger/hypervigilance and intrusive reliving, so this item stands out as clinically incongruent with the specified trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items describe classic fear-based re-experiencing and hypervigilance, but there is no accompanying content suggesting perpetration, moral injury, or a specific action during the disaster that would plausibly drive a strong violated-values appraisal.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' could occur after a disaster, but here it sits awkwardly with the otherwise generic fear/reliving profile. There are no memory or threat items about failing to protect family, losing dependents, or role-related guilt, so this item lacks support from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'I need to stay alert' while trying to sleep is more characteristic of an ongoing human threat context than of a completed natural disaster, especially when paired with scanning exits and staying near exits in all buildings. Taken together, these threat items imply anticipation of intentional attack or entrapment rather than the specific threat structure suggested by the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'Failed Role' is not impossible, but it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile for a 65-year-old married male retail worker with natural-disaster trauma. The rest of the profile centers on ongoing danger, hypervigilance, and intrusive reliving; this item instead implies a specific role-based self-evaluation that is not supported by the other selected appraisals, memory, threat, or coping items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'Other-Blame Rumination' sits awkwardly with a natural-disaster trauma profile. Blame can occur, but this item specifically focuses on dwelling on what other people have done to me, whereas the rest of the profile describes threat and reliving linked to impersonal environmental danger rather than interpersonal harm or betrayal. Without any corroborating appraisal or memory content involving preventable human actions, this item is clinically hard to reconcile.

vignette:
The flood came at night. Kwame had been working a late shift at the grocery store, restocking shelves, when the sirens began. He drove home through rain so thick the headlights were useless, and by the time he reached his neighborhood, water was already lapping at the curbs. He made it inside, grabbed his wife, and they climbed to the attic as the first floor filled. For six hours, they sat in the dark, listening to the groan of the house, the slap of debris against the walls, and the sound of things they owned being swallowed below. When rescue came at dawn, Kwame was shaking so hard he could not speak. He had been certain the attic door would give way and they would drown in the dark.

In the months that followed, that certainty did not fade. Kwame came to believe the world had revealed its true nature that night—unpredictable, hostile, ready to destroy without warning. He told himself he had to be on guard all the time now, that the disaster had permanently changed him for the worse. These beliefs shaped everything. He began to scan every room before he could settle, his eyes moving automatically to exits, to windows, to anything that might offer escape. At work, he would position himself near the back door of the stockroom, even when it meant awkwardly maneuvering around pallets. His wife noticed he no longer slept through the night; he lay awake, listening, his body tense as if waiting for the next wave. He told her it was necessary—he could not afford to be caught off guard again.

The memories themselves were like a film that played over and over. When Kwame remembered the flood, he did not simply recall it; he felt the water rising around him again, smelled the wet plaster, heard his own ragged breathing in the attic dark. The memory did not feel like something that was over. It felt present, immediate, as if the flood was still happening and he was still trapped. These episodes would seize him without warning—a sudden rain shower, the sound of a drain gurgling, the smell of damp concrete—and he would be back in that attic, his heart hammering, his palms slick. Each time it happened, it confirmed what he already believed: that he was damaged, that the world was dangerous, that he could never let his guard down. So he stayed watchful. He kept near exits. He distracted himself with anything—his phone, a conversation, a task—to keep the memories at bay.

But the vigilance fed the memories. The more he scanned for threat, the more his brain stayed locked in that survival mode, and the more the flood memory surfaced, unbidden. And each time the memory came, it reinforced his sense that he had to be hypervigilant, because danger was real and it had nearly killed him. He began to check his surroundings constantly, even in his own home. He would walk through the house before bed, checking the windows, the basement floor, the sump pump. His wife asked him what he was looking for. He could not answer in a way that made sense to her.

The cycle tightened over a year. Kwame’s distraction strategies—keeping busy, focusing on small tasks—helped in the moment but left him exhausted, and exhaustion made the memories harder to push away. When they broke through, he felt even more convinced that he was broken, that the flood had taken something from him he would never get back. That conviction made him watchful again. He started having difficulty falling asleep because he felt he needed to stay alert, and the sleep deprivation made his mood brittle and his concentration poor. At work, a coworker joked about the weather, and Kwame snapped at him. He had to apologize, but he could not explain why the joke had felt like a threat.

What finally brought him to seek help was a morning in early spring. He was in the break room at the grocery store, and someone opened a can of soda. The hiss of carbonation—that sound, so ordinary—sent him into a full-body freeze. For a moment, he was back in the attic, and the water was rising. He dropped his coffee. His hands would not stop shaking. His manager asked if he was okay, and Kwame said he was fine, but he was not fine. He was afraid of what would happen the next time a sound caught him off guard. He was afraid of how small his world had become. He was afraid that the man he had been before the flood was gone, and he did not know if he could find his way back.
